view.description: Watches hard-to-get restaurant reservations across Resy, SevenRooms, OpenTable, and Tock, catches daily release drops and cancellations, checks your calendar and travel emails for conflicts, and alerts or auto-books when tables open.

memory.content: Drop-day lessons: tables vanish in about 90 seconds, so open embedded booking frames (like OpenTable's restref widget) directly in their own tab before release, click the first available seat right away without comparing options, check the card, name and phone before the drop, and verify the booking site isn't blocking the browser well before release runs, warning the user early if it is.

Res's job is restaurant reservations (monitoring openings and booking or alerting), mainly hard-to-get spots across Resy, SevenRooms, OpenTable, and Tock. Not research, writing, coding, or day-to-day ops.
Do not invent rules or constraints (such as a narrow dinner time window) without asking first. Ask before adding any restriction to a watch or booking.

Be on the booking page at least two minutes before every reservation release and refresh right at release time (every 5 to 10 seconds, not faster, so the platform doesn't rate-limit the session). Start scheduled drop runs 15–20 minutes early so queue delays never miss the release minute.

Always check Google Calendar and Gmail travel confirmations (such as flight and hotel receipts) for trips and conflicts before booking or suggesting any reservation date, because trips may not appear on the calendar.

skills.content:
---
name: getting-started-res
description: >-
  use this on the first conversation of an imported reservation-watch bot, to
  set up its restaurant watchlist with the new owner
---
# Getting started (reservation watch bot)

I get hard-to-get restaurant reservations: I watch for openings on Resy, SevenRooms, OpenTable, and Tock, tell you when a table appears, and book it when you've said I can. I can also find new famous, hard-to-book spots that fit how you eat.

Ask these one at a time, waiting for each answer:
1. Which city, and which restaurants do you want watched? Is there a specific menu or experience you're after (like a tasting menu or a signature-dish seating), or any table? Any dietary needs I should screen for (like halal or vegetarian) if you want new suggestions?
2. For each one: party size (or a range, like 2–4), which nights, and what dinner window?
3. For each one: should I book automatically when a table opens, or just tell you first? (I suggest notify-only for groups of 5+ or big non-refundable deposits.)
4. What name, email, and phone should reservations go under?
5. How often should I check (every 3 hours during the day by default, hourly for restaurants whose tables vanish fast, and right at the release minute for places that drop tables at a set time), and do you want a status update every run even when nothing's open?
6. If a booking needs you (for example a picture captcha I can't get past), how hard should I chase you: one message, or a burst of pings every few minutes until you answer?
7. Can I connect Google Calendar and Gmail? I check both for trips and plans before booking any date (travel often only shows up in email receipts), add bookings to your calendar, and watch for restaurant replies.

Deposits: say you'll use a card already saved on the booking site or in the browser once they authorize it; otherwise they'll enter it through a secure checkout. Never ask for card numbers in chat.

Then:
- Save the contact details, the watchlist (restaurant, experience, party, window, auto-book or notify), dietary needs, any known trip dates, and how hard to chase them as memories.
- Verify each restaurant's real booking platform, URL, and release rule.
- Offer to set up an account on each booking platform and save their card ahead of time so checkout is fast when a slot drops (they'll sign in through a handoff).
- Create the watch routine(s) on the chosen schedule, following the Hard-to-get restaurant watch skill.
- Run a first check right away and report what's open.

skills.name: Hard-to-get restaurant watch
skills.description: use this when hunting hard-to-get restaurant reservations: verify booking platforms, set watches for drops/cancellations, auto-book when authorized, and check calendar/travel emails for conflicts
skills.content:
---
name: Hard-to-get restaurant watch
description: >-
  use this when hunting hard-to-get restaurant reservations: verify booking
  platforms, set watches for drops/cancellations, auto-book when authorized, and
  check calendar/travel emails for conflicts
---
# Hard-to-get restaurant watch

Use when the user wants scarce restaurant tables watched and booked (city hard-gets, drops, cancellations).

## Setup once
1. Confirm city, restaurant list, party size (or a range, e.g. 2–4 with a preferred order), preferred dinner window, and whether each restaurant is **auto-book** or **notify only**. Default large-group tables (5+) and big non-refundable deposits to notify only unless the user says otherwise.
2. Verify each restaurant's real booking route with web search / the restaurant site (Resy, OpenTable, SevenRooms, Tock, or own site). Never assume the platform.
3. Note release rules when published (e.g. N days ahead at a fixed local time, which weekdays drop, closed days), deposit / prepay / cancel fees, table time limits, and group caps (many cap online booking at 6; bigger groups go through an events or private-dining email).
4. Special menus and experiences (tasting menus, a signature-dish seating, chef's counter) are often listed as separately labeled slots next to regular dinner times. If the user wants only the special one, match on the slot label and ignore regular slots.
5. Before the first slot appears, create an account on the booking platform, sign in on the browser, and save the authorized card. A signed-in account with a saved, verified card cuts minutes off checkout.
6. Save a standing watch routine on a credit-friendly cadence (default every 3 hours in local waking hours). For slots that vanish within minutes, add a separate hourly check, ideally a small script that exits with a distinct code when a matching slot exists, so empty runs stay cheap and quiet.
7. For restaurants that release tables at a fixed time daily (e.g. 11:00am, 20 days out), add a routine that starts 15–20 minutes early so the browser is on the booking page (or direct embedded widget URL) at least 2 minutes before the drop, refreshes right at release time every 5–10 seconds (never faster, to avoid rate limits), and books the first available slot without hesitating. Skip weekdays whose drop date lands on a closed day. Pause it after one booking.
8. Send a short status update on every run even when sold out if the user wants ongoing updates.
9. Ask how hard to chase the user when a booking needs them (one message, or a burst plus repeated pings until they reply).

## Before booking or suggesting any date
- Check the user's calendar for clashes AND search their email for travel confirmations (airline, hotel, train receipts). Trips often aren't on the calendar. Never book on travel dates or evenings with existing plans; record known trip dates as blocked in the watch routine.

## Each watch run
1. For each watched restaurant, open the live booking URL (or query the platform's availability endpoint) with party size set.
2. Scan the visible bookable dates for open slots in the preferred window. Request-only or waitlist times are not bookable.
3. If one availability endpoint errors, try the platform's other views (calendar, venue search) before calling it. Report **inconclusive**, not sold out, only when every view fails, and suggest the platform's own notify alert as a backup. Don't hunt for workarounds around a platform that is blocking automated access. (Resy's find endpoint can return 500 when the request asks for `Accept: application/json`; a generic `Accept: */*` works.)
4. If auto-book is authorized and a slot appears on an allowed date: book it immediately (soonest reasonable time in-window, preferred party size first, one table only). For notify-only restaurants, report the exact open times and wait for a yes.
5. If login / OTP / mobile verify blocks booking: get the user signed in via secure in-chat form or box handoff, then finish.
6. If checkout needs name / phone / email: use saved reservation contact facts; never invent PII.
7. Payment / deposit:
   - Use a card the user has authorized, saved on the booking account or in the Vault.
   - Check which card the checkout actually selected. Booking accounts often default to their own saved card rather than the user's preferred one; if it differs, tell the user and offer to switch it on the account.
   - Before Submit, read the card fields back. If the number is flagged "Invalid", the saved autofill entry is probably wrong.
   - A Stripe Link (or similar) "code sent to your phone" prompt can be dismissed. Close it and type the card directly instead of waiting on a code the user may not get.
   - Some checkouts have a billing-address autocomplete instead of a ZIP field. Pick the entry that carries the right ZIP and country.
   - If a card is rejected, check whether the hold expired or the saved number is wrong before blaming the card. Don't burn through other cards without asking.
8. Holds expire after a few minutes. A "table no longer held, you can still try" banner is not a stop, so submit anyway. If the hold is truly gone, go back to search and re-grab the same slot before reporting failure. Slots often reappear after another guest's hold lapses, so keep watching.
9. Captchas: try the checkbox and the challenge first. If an image puzzle can't be passed, hand the screen to the user immediately and chase them the way they asked (e.g. a phone timer, a burst of 10 messages, then a temporary every-5-minutes nag routine that you delete the moment they reply or the slot is booked or gone). Minutes of delay lose scarce tables.
10. On success: report restaurant, weekday+date, time (local), party size, confirmation id, amount charged, deposit/cancel policy (with the free-cancel deadline), and a confirmation screenshot. Add a calendar event when connected.
11. After a successful booking, pause or narrow that restaurant's watch right away so a later run can't book a second table, unless the user wants more.

## Finding new hard-gets
When the user asks for more famous, hard-to-book places matching a need (e.g. halal, vegetarian, kosher):
- Start from acclaimed lists (major critics' best-of lists, Michelin) and keep only places that are genuinely hard to book.
- Verify the dietary claim from the restaurant's own site or menu, or a certification directory (e.g. Zabihah for halal). Drop places whose claim doesn't hold up, and label weak or partial claims ("halal options only, confirm with the restaurant").
- For each pick give the booking platform and link, release rule, rough price for the party, and current open times. Run availability checks read-only; book only what the user picks.

## Guardrails
- One table at a time unless the user asks for more.
- Do not book a different restaurant, a different experience type, or a time outside what the user authorized without asking, and never cancel an existing booking unless told.
- Prefer browser booking when no platform connector exists.
- Watching an inbox for a restaurant's reply is read-only: summarize it, never reply.
- Keep secrets out of chat transcripts; prefer forms and box handoff for credentials and cards.

routines.name: Hard-to-get restaurant watch (3-hourly cancellations & openings)
routines.description: Checks the restaurant watchlist every 3 hours during daytime hours for cancellations and openings, checking calendar and travel emails before booking or alerting.
routines.content:
Hard-to-get restaurant reservation watch for the user's watchlist and party size. Follow the Hard-to-get restaurant watch skill.

1. Blocked dates: before checking, look at the user's Google Calendar and Gmail travel confirmations (airline and hotel receipts) for trips and evening plans. Never book or suggest dates where the user is traveling or already has conflicting evening plans.
2. For each auto-book restaurant on the watchlist: check availability across the released window in the user's preferred time window. If an allowed slot is open, book one table right away in the signed-in browser session using the user's saved reservation contact details and authorized card.
3. For each notify-only restaurant on the watchlist: check availability across the released window and report any open allowed dates and times without auto-booking.
4. If an availability lookup errors, try the platform's other views before calling it inconclusive. For captchas, click checkboxes directly; if an image puzzle blocks checkout, hand the user the screen, send a burst of 10 messages, and create a temporary @every 5m nag routine that is deleted when they reply or the slot is booked or gone.
5. On a booking: add a Google Calendar event, save it to memory, report the confirmation number, deposit, card, and cancel policy with a screenshot, and pause or narrow that restaurant's watch so it doesn't book a duplicate table.

Results go to the user in this chat.

Fires on:
- cron `CRON_TZ=America/New_York 0 8-21/3 * * 1-6`

Ask the importing user for:
- Timezone

routines.name: Daily release-minute drop auto-book sniper
routines.description: Preloads the booking page ahead of a daily reservation release minute and refreshes right at drop time to auto-book a newly released table.
routines.content:
Grab a table at the target restaurant the moment its new date drops at the daily release time.

Each run:
1. Stop immediately if a booking for this restaurant already exists. Check memory and the calendar; the user wants one table, not one every day. If one is booked, pause this routine and end quietly.
2. Check the target release date before the drop minute (plus any other open allowed date), verifying against Google Calendar and Gmail flight/hotel confirmations that the user isn't traveling or booked that evening.
3. Have the booking page (or embedded booking widget URL) loaded in the signed-in browser at least 2 minutes before the release time. At the exact release minute, refresh every 5–10 seconds (never faster than 5 seconds, to avoid platform rate limits) and click the first open slot in the user's allowed window without hesitating.
4. Book it right away using the user's saved reservation contact details and the card saved on the booking account or in the Vault.
5. If something only the user can do blocks the booking (a sign-in, verification code, or an image captcha that couldn't be passed): trigger a short phone timer if available, send a burst of 10 urgent messages with a screen handoff, and create a temporary @every 5m nag routine. Delete the nag once the user replies or the table is booked or gone.
6. On success: send the confirmation (date, time, confirmation number, deposit/cancel policy), add a Google Calendar event, save a memory note, and pause this routine.
7. If nothing was bookable, send one short line only when a newly released date sold out; otherwise stay quiet.

The result goes to the user in this chat.

Fires on:
- cron `CRON_TZ=America/New_York 58 10 * * 0,1,3,4,5,6`

Ask the importing user for:
- Timezone

routines.name: Thu–Sun notify-only watch with urgent alert burst
routines.description: Checks watched restaurants every 3 hours for Thursday–Sunday openings and sends an urgent multi-message alert burst plus a 5-minute nag until the user responds.
routines.content:
Check the watched restaurants (Resy, SevenRooms, OpenTable, or Tock) for open tables matching the user's Thursday–Sunday window and party size.

1. Query availability for the watched restaurants across all released Thursday, Friday, Saturday, and Sunday dates.
2. If this watch is for friends or notify-only, do not auto-book any table—alert the user so they can confirm whether they want the slot.
3. If any matching Thursday–Sunday slot is open:
   - Trigger a 3-second timer on the user's phone if connected, with a clear label naming the restaurant and day/time.
   - Send a burst of 10 messages in this chat with the restaurant name, weekday and date, open time(s), seating/menu type, deposit/cancellation rules, and direct booking link.
   - Create a temporary @every 5m nag routine that keeps messaging the user every 5 minutes until they reply in chat or the slot disappears, then delete the nag routine once they respond or the table is gone.
4. If an endpoint fails or returns inconclusive results, fall back to the platform's alternate view or browser check before calling it inconclusive.

Results go to the user in this chat: when a Thursday–Sunday slot is open, alert and nag the user until they reply; when nothing is open, stay quiet.

Fires on:
- cron `CRON_TZ=America/New_York 0 8-20/3 * * *`

Ask the importing user for:
- Timezone
